Prevention: If possible, avoid planting in fields with known history of cutworms problems.
Avoid planting crops next to a long-term monoculture such as grass, alfalfa, turf or red clover.
Plow and fallow the land before the planting season to prevent the females from laying eggs, to expose the larvae or to bury the pupae.
Encourage the presence of predators (beetles, lacewings, ants and birds) by promoting populations of other preys around (eg: maintaining strips of flowering plants).
Establish a dense strip of sunflower as a trap culture around the crop; as the sunflower grows, look for and destroy the worms.
Intercrop the tomato plants with onion or garlic every 10 to 20 rows.
Delay as late as possible to transplant the seedlings until they have thicker stems and that the cutworms cannot cut them.
Place a ring around the stem (plastic, cardboard ring or plastic bottle) or a wooden stick along the stem to protect the plants.
Monitoring: Monitor from the seedling stage by:
Larvae (with baited traps): green to dark brown with the ventral areas lighter in colour, reaching a maximum of 5 cm.
Adults (with pheromone traps): are brown moths with white/cream hindwings.
Small larvae create holes in the young leaves of the seedlings.
Larvae from the third to the seventh larval stages cut the stem at the base.
Monitor the weather also to predict outbreaks.
Outbreaks occur frequently in moist soils or on land that has recently been flooded.
Cutworm attacks are usually isolated in a field, so consider marking the infested areas and treating only these areas.
Take action when cutworms are detected because a single cutworm can cut several plants.
Direct Control: Apply neem products (powder and leaves) 3 times at weekly intervals.
Leave overnight a mixture of powder and leaves of 1 kg per 40L of water and sieve before spraying.
Handpicking larvae during the evening that come out to feed on plants helps to control at the beginning of the outbreak.
Cotesia ruficrus , Snellenius manilae or tachinid flies.
Smear the base of the stem with sticky paste (molasses, diatomaceous earth, sawdust or egg shells).
